questions.question: In Python, what does a single leading underscore (for example `_balance`) on an attribute mean?
options: The attribute is a class variable.
The attribute is strictly private and cannot be accessed from outside.
A convention signalling the attribute is internal, with no access enforcement by the language.
questions.explanation: Python has no hard private keyword. A single underscore is a convention meaning do not touch this from outside. A double underscore triggers name mangling, which discourages access but still does not truly forbid it.
questions.misconception: Python encapsulation is by convention, not enforcement. The underscore signals intent; it does not lock the attribute.

questions.scenario: Two variables point at the same list: `b = a`. You append to `b`, and `a` changes too.
questions.question: Why does this happen?
options: `a` and `b` are two references to the same list object, so mutating through one is visible through the other.
Python copies the list on assignment, so this should not happen.
Lists are immutable, so neither should change.
questions.explanation: Assignment binds a new name to the same object; it does not copy. Both names reference one list, so an in-place mutation shows through both. Use `a.copy()` or `list(a)` for an independent shallow copy.
questions.misconception: Assignment never copies the object. It copies the reference, so mutations are shared.

questions.question: What is the difference between an instance variable and a static (class) variable?
options: A class variable is unique per object; an instance variable is shared.
Class variables cannot be read by instances.
An instance variable is unique per object; a class variable is shared by every instance of the class.
questions.explanation: An instance variable, set on `self`, holds per-object state. A class variable, defined in the class body, is one value shared across all instances, which suits a shared counter or a constant. Instances can read a class variable through `self` unless they shadow it.
